why_this_prefix_and_not_another.chosen: runtime-custody/ inside the MR-002 sealed evidence bucket
reasoning: the sealed bucket is the program's evidence store, versioned, with DenyInsecureTransport in force and s3:PutBucketVersioning denied at the bucket level so versioning cannot be switched off
the evaluator host role is denied s3:* on this bucket by DenyAllAccessToTheSealedStore, so placing the runtime here grants that host no new access to it

a DEDICATED non-holdout prefix is the correct categorisation signal: a numerical runtime is not holdout material and must not inherit the holdout read-Denies, which would block the custody and audit verification this artifact exists to support

explicitly_rejected.validation/ or oos/ prefixes: would miscategorise a runtime artifact as holdout material and would make it unreadable to the custody principals who need to verify it
explicitly_rejected.a registry push to ECR: would have been the tidy answer to 'not under registry custody', but a push routes the artifact through a daemon, and this workstation's containerd store demonstrably re-presents image identity. Pushing the ALREADY-VERIFIED archive as bytes keeps the chain daemon-free and self-authenticating. A registry copy remains a reasonable ADDITIONAL control later, and if taken it must record its new manifest digest SEPARATELY and never as equal to any prior registry identity.

identity_verification_from_the_custody_c.method: downloaded by pinned VersionId from the custody location and recomputed independently — not inherited from the staging verification

transport_identity.what_it_is: the S3 object's byte identity — transport custody only

docker_config_identity.what_it_is: the GOVERNED runtime identity — the Docker image specification defines image identity as the SHA-256 of the image configuration JSON

identity_verification_from_the_custody_c.kept_separate_deliberately: VersionId / retention identity and Docker config identity are DIFFERENT identifiers answering different questions — 'which stored object' versus 'which runtime'. They are recorded in separate fields and must never be written as if one implied the other.

findings.severity: open control gap — NOT closed by this record
findings.title: The sealed bucket's deletion Deny is prefix-scoped and does not protect runtime-custody/.
findings.statement: The live bucket policy (identity 7bb73e62066e52303c5d48ed0cd740cb16b4f2825110dde92d9cc4d6dfc164a5, verified equal to the Amendment R sealed value recorded at ab78bb5, so the policy is unchanged since that amendment) contains DenyPermanentDeletionOfSealedObjectVersions scoped to: the bucket itself for s3:PutBucketVersioning, plus validation/* and oos/* object versions. runtime-custody/* is NOT among them. The custody object's versions are therefore deletable by an administrative principal.
findings.what_would_close_it: adding arn:aws:s3:::workbench-mr002-sealed-219024422756/runtime-custody/* to the Resource list of that ONE existing statement. It grants nothing, removes no read access from anyone, and extends only deletion protection.
findings.why_it_is_NOT_applied_here: This is the same bucket-policy surface whose quiet mis-scoping cost the program a governed latch cycle on 2026-08-21 — a complete, correct identity-side amendment defeated by the resource side nobody had re-pointed. The program's own Amendment R procedure exists for this: seal the amendment before applying it, ENUMERATE every top-level element, and REFUSE if any element other than the intended one changes. Applying a policy change to that surface unilaterally, at the end of a long session, is exactly the shortcut that history argues against.
recommended_procedure_if_approved: seal the proposed document and its identity BEFORE application

diff every top-level element (Version, Id, and all four Sids) and refuse on any unintended change — note that the live policy already HAS an Id (MR002SealedStorePolicy), so a naive draft that writes an Id would REPLACE it, which is the precise defect Amendment R caught in itself
re-verify latch 8/CLOSED and that no read-Deny scope changed

findings.title: The artifact now exists in three independent places; the single-failure-domain risk from F4 is gone.
findings.statement: Copies: (1) the evaluator host's local Docker image store and its 08-18 runtime_custody tar, both on i-00c1034f7026db45e's EBS volume; (2) the staging object in workbench-backups-219024422756, version-pinned; (3) the custody object in workbench-mr002-sealed-219024422756, version-pinned. Copies 2 and 3 are in different buckets and are each independently self-authenticating, because each contains the config object whose own hash is the bound identity.
findings.consequence_for_F4: F4's catastrophic component — loss of one EBS volume making the runtime behind both consumed holdouts permanently unreproducible — is RESOLVED. F4's governance component — the artifact is under no durable custody control — is reduced to the deletion-Deny gap in P1-CUST-F1 and remains OPEN until that is closed.
